Before the first day: Building psychological safety into pre-boarding

In the third installment of her series on psychological safety, Helen Sanderson looks at pre-boarding, setting out how HR can strengthen each of the Five Foundations between offer and start date, and what to review first.
  • By Helen Sanderson
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 6:41
Instaread

Summary: Psychological safety is experienced in teams, and the everyday systems an organisation runs either support it or work against it. Pre-boarding is the quietest of those systems and the easiest to leave to chance. Here’s how HR can strengthen each of the Five Foundations during this crucial stage.

Pre-boarding covers the weeks between someone accepting an offer and starting work. The person has committed to a job they have not yet done, in a team they have not yet worked with, on the basis of what they were told during recruitment. What happens during those weeks either confirms that account or quietly contradicts it, and the person notices either way.

Neil Eastwood, a recruitment expert who advised us at Wellbeing Teams, drew on Skills for Care data from the social care workforce to show that the period between offer and start date is when people are most likely to change their mind [1]. We had not realised how important that stage was, and we lost people because of it.

For HR, this stage is visible only in data from other stages of the employee journey. Probation extensions linked to expectations nobody confirmed, first-week feedback about feeling unprepared and questions asked in week one that could have been answered four weeks earlier all begin here, and none of them are recorded here. 

Designing these pre-boarding weeks, instead of leaving them to administration, confirms what recruitment described and adds what someone needs in order to start well.

The Five Foundations in pre-boarding

The Five Foundations of psychological safety are Mattering, Clarity, Voice, Connection and Learning. They name the questions people are answering, often without realising it, in their everyday work.

Mattering asks whether I count here, and during pre-boarding it is expressed almost entirely through the reliability of communication.

Confirming start details, sending information in advance and acknowledging milestones all signal attentiveness, and silence is read as an indication of what the organisation will be like to work for.

The period between offer and start date is when people are most likely to change their mind

What Mattering can look like in practice

In Wellbeing Teams, new colleagues were invited into our Slack group within 24 hours of accepting a role. Over the following four weeks, while checks and references were processed, we ran a deliberate sequence: a personal text from the Wellbeing Leader, who would be their team leader, a small gift sent through the post in the first week and a handwritten postcard of our 10 promises to colleagues two weeks later. 

We also sent a couple of questions each week, to learn about our new colleagues and to answer theirs. Each of these came from the line manager. A manager with one or two new starters can do this whatever the size of the organisation. 

Buckingham and Coffman, drawing on Gallup interviews with more than 80,000 managers across 400 companies and a range of industries, found that how long someone stays is shaped most by the relationship with their immediate manager [2]. Pre-boarding is where that relationship starts.

Gaining Clarity

Clarity answers the question of what is expected of me here and how things work in practice. 

By the end of pre-boarding, a new starter should be able to answer three questions: 

  1. What success in the first month involves.
  2. Who decides day-to-day priorities.
  3. Who to ask when something is unclear.

What Voice looks like

Voice answers a practical question: can I raise concerns, ask questions or disagree without it harming my standing here? 

Someone who has accepted an offer and has not yet started has every reason to stay quiet. So a scheduled conversation with their manager before day one is more than an open invitation. 

Recurring themes from those conversations show where the briefing materials need work.

How long someone stays is shaped most by the relationship with their immediate manager

Connection: a relational question

Connection answers a relational question: do I know what to expect from people here? 

Introducing relational context before arrival is what strengthens it. Where a team has Team Agreements, sharing them in advance shows the behaviours the team has agreed they want from each other.

Learning and experience

Learning answers a simple question: do we learn from experience? The evidence at this stage comes from new starters and their managers. 

Where the same questions recur across several starters, the materials can be adjusted before the next recruitment cycle.

Start by reviewing the pre-boarding in one part of the organisation, choosing where offers are declined late or where probation extensions reference expectations nobody confirmed. 

Where there are many hires, the sequence can be written once and used by every manager, so what each manager adds is the personal contact. 

The cost is mostly diary time, about an hour per starter across four weeks and most of it the manager’s, and the work it removes is the first fortnight spent answering questions that could have been answered earlier.

Actionable insights for HR

1. Give the period between offer and start date a named owner. It sits between recruitment and induction, which is why it goes unowned. Name who is responsible for contact during those weeks, what they will send and when.

2. Send the role descriptions again with the start date, and name the first month. Set out what success in month one involves, and who decides day-to-day priorities.

3. Schedule one conversation with the manager before day one. Put it in both diaries at the offer stage, and use it to invite questions instead of giving information that could have been sent.

4. Share the team’s behavioural expectations before arrival. Where Team Agreements exist, send them with an explanation of how they are used. Otherwise set out how the team handles feedback, disagreement and decisions, so none of it has to be worked out by watching.

5. Ask new starters in their first week what they wish they had known. Ask through someone other than their manager, since week one is when people are trying to make a good impression, and change the pack where the same gap appears twice.

Notes

1. Eastwood, N (2017) Saving Social Care, Rethink Press, and Skills for Care (2023) The State of the Adult Social Care Sector and Workforce in England, Skills for Care, Leeds

2. Buckingham, M and Coffman, C (1999) First, Break All the Rules: What the world’s greatest managers do differently, Simon and Schuster, New York

Helen Sanderson is the author of Psychological Safety in Practice (Kogan Page, 2026).
